author: Ahmed Ibrahim
title: American Dream Sunday Shopping Lawsuit | NBC New York
text:
American Dream Mall Sued Over Alleged Violation of New Jersey’s ‘Blue Laws’ A legal challenge has been filed against the American Dream mall in New Jersey, alleging the sprawling entertainment and retail complex has been illegally selling nonessential items on Sundays.The lawsuit, brought by officials in Paramus, New Jersey, centers on the state’s antiquated “blue laws” and raises questions about competitive fairness and promises made to local communities.
The suit contends that American Dream, located in East Rutherford, is flouting a Bergen County law that prohibits the sale of items like clothing, appliances, and furniture on Sundays. While the mall offers a wide array of attractions – including an indoor ski slope, surfing simulator, and roller coasters – it’s the retail component that’s now under legal scrutiny.
These blue laws , remnants of a bygone era, have roots in religious observance dating back centuries in New Jersey. However, modern supporters argue they provide a much-needed respite from the congestion and noise that plague the region, particularly given its proximity to New York City and the constant influx of shoppers throughout the week.
According to officials in Paramus, a important shopping destination boasting numerous malls and strip malls, the vast majority of retail stores in the county adhere to the Sunday closure rule. “Nearly every other retail store in the county is closed to shoppers on Sundays,” a local official stated.
The original understanding surrounding American Dream’s opening in 2019,adjacent to MetLife Stadium,was that retail stores would remain closed on sundays,while the entertainment venues would continue to operate. Though, a report published by NorthJersey.com in January revealed that retailers within the mall had been opening their doors on Sundays for nearly a year.
“These businesses, with the encouragement and support of the mall’s ownership and the acquiescence of the other defendants here, have violated the law hundreds if not thousands of times sence January,” the lawsuit alleges, as filed in state Superior Court.
American Dream has countered the claims, asserting that the Bergen County blue laws do not apply to the complex due to its location on state-owned property. In a statement, the mall characterized the lawsuit as “a meritless political stunt driven by private competitors’ interests.”
Though, Paramus Mayor Christopher DiPiazza refuted this claim, stating that American Dream had “promised on record” to comply with the county’s blue laws upon opening.Evidence supporting this assertion comes from a 2011 public hearing transcript,where tony armlin,then a vice president with mall owner Triple Five,acknowledged that the laws “prohibit our ability to have retail activities on Sundays,” citing potential traffic impacts.
Jim Tedesco, the Bergen County executive, echoed this sentiment, stating that American Dream’s operators had “personally assured” him that retail stores would remain closed on Sundays prior to the mall’s launch. “They broke that promise,” Tedesco said. “Their decision to operate retail on Sundays not only violates state statute, it gives them an unfair advantage over every other business in Bergen County that is following the law.”
The lawsuit also names the municipality of East rutherford, whose mayor has not yet responded to requests for comment, as well as the New Jersey Sports and Exposition authority. Both the NJSEA and the state attorney general’s office have declined to comment,citing the ongoing nature of the litigation.
New Jersey’s blue laws were onc far more thorough, extending beyond business operations to encompass leisure activities and even nonessential travel. Proponents at the time argued for a moral obligation to protect the Sabbath from commercialism and recreation. While most counties in New Jersey have since repealed these laws, Bergen County has consistently resisted such efforts, with voters upholding the measures, which do allow exemptions for essential services like grocery and drug stores.
The outcome of this legal battle could have significant implications for American Dream and the future of blue laws in Bergen County, possibly reshaping the retail landscape and raising questions about the balance between economic development and long-standing community regulations.
